attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new sprite kind named SmallAsteroid at the top of the editor inside the SpriteKind namespace?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How did you create a new sprite kind in the blocks editor?

❓ What keywords and symbols do you use to declare a new sprite kind in JavaScript?

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja should be familiar with the concept of sprite kinds and be able to recall creating new sprite kinds in the blocks editor. In the [set sprite to] block, the ninja was able to use the sprite kind drop down to easily type a new sprite kind. In JavaScript, the process is a little trickier as sprite kinds need to be declared in a separate namespace. This helps to organize the code and the keyword export allows the sprite kinds to be used throughout the rest of the project.

💡 Walk through the syntax of the code that declares a new sprite kind with the ninja. Make sure that they have included the correct keywords, symbols, functions, and spacing so that the new sprite kind is able to be used outside of the namespace.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by noticing that 2 sprite kinds and several code comments have already been added to the editor!


Notice the new keywords in blue: namespace and export. A namespace is a separate section of code inside curly brackets { }. The namespace will help organize code in a project, similar to code comments. However, the code inside the namespace’s block statement needs to be exported in order for it to be used in the rest of the project.


These new keywords are followed by let and the names of 2 new sprite kinds: Ship and LargeAsteroid. An assignment operator is used to create the sprite kinds using the SpriteKind.create() function. 


Add a SmallAsteroid sprite kind by creating a new line inside the namespace’s block statement, then using the keywords export and let, the name of the new sprite kind, an assignment operator, and the SpriteKind.create() function. 


Now, the 3 new sprite kinds have been declared and can be used throughout the project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a Ship sprite, set its starting position, and enable it to be controlled by direction buttons?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you use Ship as the Ship sprite’s sprite kind?

❓ Why is screen.height - ship.height / 2 used as the Ship sprite’s y-coordinate value?

❓ What should you set the vx and vy parameters to in the moveSprite code so that the Player sprite is only able to move left and right?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja how the y-coordinate of the Ship sprite is calculated. The height of the screen is 120 pixels. The height of the Ship sprite (24) is divided by 2 (12), to find its center. That value is then subtracted from the screen height (108). This places the Ship sprite just above the bottom of the screen, at the center of the Ship sprite.

💡 Remind the ninja that the vx parameter sets how quickly a sprite will move left and right on the screen. The vy parameter sets how quickly a sprite will move up and down on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a Ship sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // Ship sprite set up. Select the rocket ship image from My Assets and use ship as the sprite name. Change the sprite kind by deleting .Player then retyping the dot operator . and selecting Ship from the list of properties.


Position the Ship sprite on the bottom center of the screen. Open Sprites, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the Ship sprite, and update the x and y parameters. Use screen.width / 2 as the x value and screen.height - ship.height / 2 as the y value.


Allow the Ship sprite to move left and right along the bottom of the screen. Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the position code. Replace mySprite with the Ship sprite’s name, then update the vx and vy parameters, so that the Ship sprite is only able to move left and right.


Click ▶ to move the Ship sprite horizontally along the bottom of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the parameters in createProjectileFromSprite so that whenever the A button is pressed, a projectile launches upwards from the Ship sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which sprite should a projectile launch from?

❓ What value might you use for the vy parameter, so that a projectile is sent upward on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to make sure that they’ve used the correct sprite name in the sprite parameter of the createProjectileFromSprite code.

💡 Remind the ninja that positive vy values move the sprite downward on the screen and negative vy values move the sprite upward on the screen. Larger absolute values make the sprite move faster.
steps.instructions:
Code the Ship sprite to launch space lasers!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // ship sprite projectile, using the default property A and default event Pressed. 


Open Sprites and drag [projectile (img) from (mySprite) with vx (vx) vy (vy)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

let projectile = sprites.createProjectileFromSprite
(img` `, mySprite, 50, 50)


The createProjectileFromSprite function takes 4 parameters: img, sprite, vx, and vy. Click the palette to select the space laser image from My Assets, then replace mySprite with the Ship sprite’s name. Set vx to 0 and vy to a number that sends the space laser up.


Click ▶ then press A to launch a space laser from the Ship sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you code a LargeAsteroid projectile to appear inside a onUpdateInterval loop, and update the parameters so the LargeAsteroid projectile moves down?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How frequently should a LargeAsteroid sprite appear on screen?

❓ What value might you use for the projectile’s vy parameter, so that a projectile is sent downward on the screen?

❓ What sprite kind should the largeAsteroid sprite be assigned?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Make sure the Ninja has used the createProjectileFromSide function to send projectiles from the top of the screen, not createProjectileFromSprite, which sends projectiles from a particular sprite.

💡 Remind the ninja that positive vy values move the sprite downward on the screen and negative vy values move the sprite upward on the screen. Larger values make the sprite move faster.

💡 Point out to the ninja that the new sprite kind (LargeAsteroid) was declared at the top of the editor in the namespace. Because the keyword export was used, the sprite kind is able to be used elsewhere in the project, outside of the namespace’s curly brackets { }
steps.instructions:
Create asteroid sprites that fall from the top of the screen.


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] underneath // large asteroid sprite. Replace 500 with a value that sets how frequently a LargeAsteroid sprite will appear.


Open Sprites and drag [projectile (img) from side with vx (vx) vy (vy)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop. Rename the projectile largeAsteroid then click the palette to select the large asteroid image from My Assets. Set vx to 0 and vy to a number that sends the asteroid down.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) kind to (value)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onUpdateInterval loop, underneath the projectile code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

mySprite.setKind(SpriteKind.Player)

Replace mySprite with largeAsteroid then change the kind parameter to SpriteKind.LargeAsteroid.


Set a random x position for each LargeAsteroid sprite by using a dot operator . after the sprite name to access the x position, then using an assignment operator = and randint to place each sprite somewhere across the width of the screen.


Click ▶ to see LargeAsteroid sprites appear on the top of the screen and move down towards the Ship sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the kind parameter to Ship and otherKind parameter to LargeAsteroid in the onOverlap event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when a Ship sprite overlaps with a LargeAsteroid sprite?

❓ What handler parameter should be used in place of the sprite name so that the LargeAsteroid is destroyed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk through the sequence of the onOverlap event with the ninja. When the Ship sprite overlaps a LargeAsteroid sprite, the LargeAsteroid sprite is destroyed. 

💡 otherSprite should be used in the destroy code since SpriteKind.LargeAsteroid is used as the otherKind parameter.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when a LargeAsteroid sprite overlaps with the Ship sprite!


Open Sprites and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // large asteroid overlap code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.onOverlap(SpriteKind.Player, SpriteKind.Player, function(sprite: Sprite, otherSprite: Sprite) { })


The onOverlap event takes 3 parameters: kind, otherKind, and handler. Update the kind parameter by deleting .Player, retyping the dot operator . and selecting Ship. Change the otherKind parameter to LargeAsteroid.


Open Sprites and drag [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.destroy(mySprite)


Replace mySprite with otherSprite so the LargeAsteroid sprite is destroyed when it overlaps with the Ship sprite. 


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Ship sprite overlaps with a LargeAsteroid sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use 2 destroy functions inside the onOverlap event so that both the Projectile and LargeAsteroid sprites are destroyed when they overlap?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you use the correct sprite kinds in the parameters of the second onOverlap to the correct sprite kinds?

❓ What happens when a Projectile sprite and a LargeAsteroid sprite overlap?

❓ What parameter(s) should be used in place of sprite names in the destroy code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When a Projectile sprite overlaps a LargeAsteroid sprite, both sprites are destroyed.

💡 sprite and otherSprite should be used in the destroy code, so that both the Projectile sprite and the LargeAsteroid sprite are destroyed on overlap.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when a Projectile sprite overlaps a LargeAsteroid sprite!


Open Sprites and drag a second [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // large asteroid overlap code.


The onOverlap event takes 3 parameters: kind, otherKind, and handler. Update the kind parameter by deleting .Player, retyping the dot operator . and selecting Projectile. Change the otherKind parameter to LargeAsteroid.


Open Sprites and drag 2 [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of the second onOverlap event. Replace mySprite with sprite in the first destroy code, and with otherSprite in the other, so both the LargeAsteroid and Projectile sprites are destroyed whenever they overlap. 


Click ▶ to see what happens when a Projectile sprite overlaps a LargeAsteroid sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 2 new SmallAsteroid sprites at the position where the LargeAsteroid sprite was destroyed by using otherSprite.x and otherSprite.y as parameters?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you use SmallAsteroid as the sprite kind for the SmallAsteroid sprites?

❓ Why is otherSprite used in the code that sets the SmallAsteroid sprites’ positions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the new sprite kind SmallAsteroid was declared at the top of the editor in the namespace. Because the keyword export was used, the sprite kind is able to be used elsewhere in the project, outside of the namespace’s curly brackets { }

💡 Walk through the logic of the SmallAsteroid sprites’ position code. When a Projectile sprite overlaps a LargeAsteroid sprite, both sprites are destroyed and 2 Small Asteroid sprites are created. Their x and y-coordinates are set to the same position as the otherSprite (the LargeAsteroid sprite), so that they appear in the spot where the LargeAsteroid overlaps the Projectile sprite.
steps.instructions:
Make the LargeAsteroid sprite "break" into 2 SmallAsteroid sprites when it is struck by a Projectile.


Open Sprites and drag 2 [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath the existing code inside the Projectile/LargeAsteroid onOverlap event. Select the small asteroid image from My Assets for both lines of code, then use a different sprite name for each sprite. Change the kind parameter to SmallAsteroid for both sprites.


Use otherSprite to position the SmallAsteroid sprites where the LargeAsteroid sprite was when it was destroyed. Open Sprites, drag 2 [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the SmallAsteroid sprites, and update the sprite names in both lines of code. For both sprites, use otherSprite.x as the x parameter and otherSprite.y as the y parameter.


Click ▶ to see 2 SmallAsteroid sprites appear in the same position as the LargeAsteroid sprite after it’s been struck by a Projectile.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the SmallAsteroid sprite kind in the onCreated event, then use sprite to set the velocity of each SmallAsteroid sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using an onCreated event in JavaScript similar and different than the blocks editor?

❓ Which parameter should be used as the sprite name in the code inside the onCreated event?

❓ Once created, in what direction will the SmallAsteroid sprites move in?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the [on created] container that they used in the blocks editor. Similarly to JavaScript, the sprite kind was specified in the kind parameter. Because there is only 1 kind parameter, sprite should be used in the code inside the event’s block statement.

💡 Once created, the SmallAsteroid sprites will move down and to the right, because the vx and vy values are positive.
steps.instructions:
Code the 2 SmallAsteroid sprites to move in different directions when they are created!


Open Sprites, drag [run code on created (sprite) of kind (kind)] underneath // small asteroid sprite. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

sprites.onCreated(SpriteKind.Player, function(sprite: Sprite) { })

The onCreated event takes 2 parameters: kind, and handler. Change the kind to SmallAsteroid. 


Use sprite to set the velocity of each SmallAsteroid sprite when it is created. Set random vx and vy values by using a dot operator . after sprite, then using an assignment operator = and randint to set the speed between 20 and 40.


Click ▶ to see the SmallAsteroid sprites appear and then move diagonally across the screen when a LargeAsteroid sprite is struck by a Projectile.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use Math.percentChance and a multiplication assignment operator *= to code the SmallAsteroid sprites to move in all 4 directions on the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How is the multiplication assignment operator similar to other assignment operators previously used?

❓ Once created, in what direction will the SmallAsteroid sprites move in? Why?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they can access the asterisk on their keyboard by pressing the Shift + 8 keys at the same time.

💡 Similarly to the addition or subtraction assignment operators, the multiplication assignment operator takes the value on the left side of the operator and multiplies it by the value on the right side of the operator. The value on the left is then assigned the updated value.

💡 Once created, the SmallAsteroid sprites may move in any of the 4 directions, because there is a 50% chance that the vx and vy values are positive, and 50% chance that the vx and vy values are negative.
steps.instructions:
Code the SmallAsteroid sprites to move in all 4 directions on the screen.


Currently, the SmallAsteroid sprites only move down and to the right because the vx and vy values are positive numbers. By multiplying these values by -1, they can be turned into negative numbers which move up and to the left.


Open Logic, drag 2 [if] under the existing code inside the curly brackets { } of the onCreated event. Delete true inside the parentheses of both if conditions. Then, open Math and drag [(percentage) % chance] inside both sets of parentheses. Replace 0 with 50 so there is a 50% chance the sprite will move in one direction and a 50% chance it will move in the opposite direction.


Inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditionals, use sprite with a dot operator . to access vx in one conditional and vy in the other. Use a multiplication assignment operator *= to multiply the vx or vy value by -1. 


Click ▶ to see the SmallAsteroid sprites move in different directions across the screen when they appear.

steps.hints: ❓Did you create 2 onOverlap events, one set to Ship/Small Asteroid, the other set to Projectile/Small Asteroid?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Ship or Projectile sprites overlap a SmallAsteroid sprite?

❓ Did you use the correct values in the kind, otherKind, and handler parameters?

❓ What values might be used for the effect and duration parameters in the destroy code?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Ship or Projectile sprites overlap a SmallAsteroid sprite, the SmallAsteroid sprite is destroyed.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation box to add additional parameters to the destroy code. Inside the parentheses, the ninja can type effects. to use the code completion tool to select an effect. Then, they can type a comma , followed by a value in milliseconds to set the duration of the effect.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the Ship or Projectile sprites overlap a SmallAsteroid sprite!


Open Sprites and drag 2 [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // small asteroid overlap code.


Update the kind parameter to Ship in one onOverlap event and Projectile in the other. Change the otherKind parameter to SmallAsteroid in both events.


Open Sprites and drag [destroy (mySprite)] inside the curly brackets { } of both onOverlap events. Replace mySprite with otherSprite so each SmallAsteroid sprite is destroyed when it overlaps a Ship or Projectile sprite. 


The destroy function takes 2 optional parameters: effects, and duration. Use the documentation box to add these parameters to the code when the Projectile overlaps the SmallAsteroid sprite.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Ship or Projectile sprites overlap a SmallAsteroid sprite!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add an info.changeLifeBy inside each onOverlap events for Ship/LargeAsteroid and Ship/SmallAsteroid, and set the parameters to different negative values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How many lives might the Ship sprite begin the project with?

❓ How many lives should be lost when the Ship sprite overlaps with LargeAsteroid and SmallAsteroid sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 There are many onOverlap events in this project; make sure the Ninja is adding code to the Ship/LargeAsteroid and Ship/SmallAsteroid events.

💡 Remind the ninja to tinker with the values in the setLife and changeLifeBy code to match each unique overlap event and to make the project playable, but challenging.
steps.instructions:
Code the Ship sprite to lose a life on overlap with asteroid sprites!


Open Info and drag [set life to (3)] underneath // game set up. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

info.setLife(3)

Tinker with the value parameter to set how many lives the Ship sprite will start with.


Open Info again and drag [change life by (-1)] underneath the destroy code inside the curly brackets { } of the onOverlap events for both the Ship/LargeAsteroid and Ship/SmallAsteroid code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

info.changeLifeBy(-1)

Set the parameter to change by a larger amount (-2) for the LargeAsteroid and a smaller amount (-1) for the SmallAsteroid.


Click ▶ to see the Ship sprite lose different amounts of life when it overlaps with a LargeAsteroid or SmallAsteroid sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use / 1000 after the game.runtime function to change this value to seconds?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the value found through the game.runtime() function divided by 1000?

❓ Does the dialog box message appear correctly when the Ship sprite runs out of lives?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the game.runtime() function will output a value in milliseconds. This number is then divided by 1000 to convert it to seconds, making it easier for the user to understand.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure the strings and number values they’ve concatenated appear correctly when the dialog box shows.
steps.instructions:
When the Ship sprite’s life reaches 0, show the user how long they survived, then reset the game.


Open Info, drag [run code on life zero] under // game over. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

info.onLifeZero(function() { })

Open Game, drag [show long text (str) (layout)] inside the curly brackets { } of onLifeZero. Replace null with a string that tells the user “You survived for “ then a + to concatenate the string with a function that will show how long the game lasted.


Open Game, drag [time since start (ms)] after the +. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

game.runtime()

The runtime function will show the time since the game began in milliseconds; type / 1000 after the function to change this value to seconds. 


Complete the dialog box by concatenating one additional string that shows “ seconds” after the runtime value. Update the position of the dialog box, too!


Open Game and drag [reset game] inside the curly brackets { } of onLifeZero underneath the showLongText code. Now, the game will reset after the user views the dialog box. 


Click ▶ to see the game time appear on screen when the Ship life reaches 0.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the Math.round function to round the runtime function to the nearest whole number?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the Math.round function do? How is it used in the dialog box text?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the ninja tested their project in the previous step, they likely were presented with a value with many digits after the decimal point. By using the Math.round function, the project will round the game run time to the nearest whole number, making it easier for the user to understand.
steps.instructions:
Use rounding to make the runtime value easier to read!


round is an example of a function that cannot be found in the code block menu, but is available using the code completion tool. To the left of the runtime function inside the showLongText code, type Math. to view all of the functions available in the Math namespace. Scroll down to select round.


The round function takes 1 parameter: a number. Type parentheses around game.runtime() / 1000 to use the value as the parameter for the round function.


Click ▶ to see the runtime rounded to the nearest whole number when the Ship sprite’s life reaches 0.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use info.setLifeImage function to change the life meter image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image might be used to show how many lives a player has?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja will need to type img`` inside the parentheses of the setLifeImage function to enable the palette to appear. The ninja can find the backtick symbol below the Esc key and to the left of the 1 on their keyboard.

💡 Make sure the ninja has selected an image that is 8x8 pixels. Otherwise, the image may not appear fully in the life variable’s box on screen.

💡 Explain to the ninja that changing the life variable’s image is another example of the greater possibilities that coding in the JavaScript editor allows for.
steps.instructions:
Change the life meter image!


setLifeImage is another example of a function that cannot be found in the code block menu, but is available using the code completion tool. On a blank line under // game set up underneath the setLife code, type info. to view all of the functions available in the info namespace. Scroll down to select setLifeImage.


The setLifeImage function takes 1 parameter: an image that is 8x8 pixels. Type a pair of parentheses () after the function name, then type img`` inside them. Click the palette to draw or select an 8x8 pixel image to replace the heart image in the life meter.


Click ▶ to see the new life meter image appear on the top left of the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ What directions would help players understand how the game is played?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game? 

❓ Which screen effect might you use to customize the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding directions and screen effects!


Open Game and drag 1 or more [splash (title)] underneath // game set up. Update the title and subtitle parameters, so that splash screens share directions for the user to follow.


Open Scene, drag [start screen (effect) effect] underneath // game set up. Use the dot operator . to select an effect from the code completion tool. Inside the parentheses, fill in the 2 parameters (duration and particlesPerSecond) to customize the screen effect. Use the documentation box for help with each parameter.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses unique sprite kinds to make things happen using sprite overlap and lifecycle events.

validationItems.text: Create a new SpriteKind named SmallAsteroid.
Create a Ship sprite, set its position, and move it with the controller.
Create and launch a Projectile sprite when the A button is pressed.
Create projectiles inside an onUpdateInterval loop that fall from the top of the screen. Set its SpriteKind to LargeAsteroid and give them random starting x positions.
When the Ship sprite overlaps with a LargeAsteroid sprite, destroy the otherSprite.
Destroy the Projectile and the LargeAsteroid sprites when they overlap each other. Create two small asteroids at the position of the large asteroid.
When created, assign SmallAsteroid sprites random x and y velocities. Use if statements to randomize their directions.
When the Ship sprite or Projectile sprites overlap with a SmallAsteroid, destroy the otherSprite.
Set the player’s life at the start of the game. Make the player lose 1 life when the Ship sprite overlaps a SmallAsteroid sprite and 2 when it overlaps a LargeAsteroid sprite.
When the player runs out of lives, display how long they survived and reset the game.
Give the player instructions and add a screen effect.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Purple Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about sprite kinds and sprite overlap events. In the JavaScript editor, you can use a namespace to create new sprite kinds. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: One of a Kind
